newsitem.title: USA: Calif. Gov. signs measure to create quake authority.
newsitem.headline: Calif. Gov. signs measure to create quake authority.

text.p: California Gov. Pete Wilson signed controversial legislation Friday to create a $10.5 billion publicly run authority to sell earthquake insurance to homeowners in the state.
Wilson, a Republican, said the legislation should help to end California's insurance availability crisis for homeowners seeking earthquake coverage.
"Earthquakes will always be a fact of life in California, but homeowners no longer must risk a devastating, unrecoverable loss because they couldn't get insurance," Wilson said.
The legislation will implement the so-called California Earthquake Authority. The proposal was approved by the legislature in August after months of heated debate.
The privately financed, publicly managed authority will provide insurance coverage for earthquake damage to residential property owners, condominium owners, mobile-home owners and renters.

The authority's earthquake policy would be limited to dwelling structures only, with a 15 percent deductible. Its policies would be written and serviced by private insurers and their agents, but the authority would issue the policy and pay the earthquake claims.
California Insurance Commissioner Chuck Quackenbush said the authority should begin to sell policies by Dec. 1.

"Gov. Wilson's signature on legislation creating the California Earthquake Authority means that California's economic recovery will proceed on course -- uninterrupted by the evaporation of homeowners' insurance and the paralysing effect that would have on the state's real estate market," Quackenbush said in a statement.
As a public entity, the authority will be tax-exempt, enabling it to build up enough reserves to cover major earthquake disasters.
The authority will be capable of funding $10.5 billion through a combination of sources, including insurer contributions, policyholder premiums, the capital markets, and reinsurance.

Quackenbush maintains that the authority would, in its first year of operation, have enough resources to pay all claims from an earthquake more than twice as destructive as the devastating 1994 Northridge quake.
Wilson said mammoth natural disasters like the Northridge quake create a magnitude of loss that can plunge an insurance company into insolvency.
Such disasters, coupled with California's requirement that homeowner policyholders be offered earthquake insurance, have severely restricted the availability of these policies, Wilson said.

The California Department of Insurance estimated that about 99 percent of California insurers had restricted or stopped selling homeowner and earthquake insurance, making it difficult for homebuyers to obtain mortgages.
"The CEA will provide much-needed relief for the insurance availablility shortage," Wilson said.
